warmup.q: A settlement reader emits 200 postings into .buffer(10). The ledger writer behind it is stuck on posting 1. How many of the reader's emit calls have returned?
options: 0: emit always waits for the collector
200: the buffer lets the reader finish
warmup.why: buffer(10) runs the reader in a second coroutine that sends into a channel with 10 slots. Postings 2 to 11 fill the slots, and posting 1 left the channel when the writer took it. That is 10 + 1. Then the next send suspends. The answer 0 is right only without a buffer, where emit calls the writer's code directly.

sections.h: A buffer is a second coroutine and a belt with n slots
sections.html:
The settlement import reads postings from the acquirer's file and writes each one to the ledger. Today a row lock holds the writer on posting 1. The reader is a plain flow { } that counts how many of its emit calls have returned. Put a buffer between them and look at the counter while the writer waits:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: a bounded queue between a reader thread and a writer thread
BlockingQueue<Integer> belt = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10);
Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { for (int seq = 1; seq <= 200; seq++) { putQuietly(belt, seq); returned.set(seq); } });
Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { while (true) ledger.post(takeQuietly(belt)); });   // stuck on posting 1
Kotlin
var returned = 0
val reader = flow { for (seq in 1..200) { emit(seq); returned = seq } }
launch { reader.buffer(10).collect { posting -> ledger.post(posting) } }   // stuck on posting 1
delay(100)
println(returned)   // and with no buffer? buffer(0)? buffer()?

Write your four guesses down. The answers are 0 with no buffer, 1 for buffer(0), 11 for buffer(10) and 65 for buffer(). They come out the same on every run.

The 0 is lesson 1 of this track: without a buffer, emit calls the writer's code, so it can't return while the writer is stuck. The other three numbers need a mechanism. The buffer KDoc sketches it in four lines, and it is worth writing out once:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: a second thread runs the upstream and puts into a queue with n slots
static <T> void handMadeBuffer(List<T> upstream, int n, Consumer<T> downstream) throws InterruptedException {
    BlockingQueue<T> belt = n == 0 ? new SynchronousQueue<>() : new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(n);
    Thread producer = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> upstream.forEach(v -> putQuietly(belt, v)));
    for (int i = 0; i < upstream.size(); i++) downstream.accept(belt.take());
    producer.join();
}
Kotlin
fun <T> Flow<T>.handMadeBuffer(n: Int): Flow<T> = flow {
    coroutineScope {
        val channel = produce(capacity = n) { collect { send(it) } }   // coroutine 2 runs the upstream
        channel.consumeEach { emit(it) }                               // our coroutine hands each value on
    }
}

Read it as two rooms with a belt with n slots between them. buffer(n) moves everything above it into a second coroutine. In there, the reader's emit has become a send into a channel, and send returns as soon as a slot is free. Our own coroutine takes values off the belt and calls the real emit, which runs the writer. So while the writer holds posting 1, postings 2 to 11 sit on the belt. Eleven emits have returned: ten for the postings on the belt, and one for posting 1, which left the belt when the writer picked it up. If this looks like the wall with a mailbox slot from lesson 3 of this track, it is the same machine: flowOn builds it to change the dispatcher, buffer builds it to change the size of the slot.

buffer(0) has no slots. It is a hand-over where both hands must meet, which channels call a rendezvous. There is still a second coroutine, so exactly one emit returns. That one value of slack is why buffer(0) turns the 1,200 ms of the 100/300 ms model from lesson 9 of the coroutines track into 1,000 ms, the same as buffer().

buffer() with no argument means Channel.BUFFERED, which is -2 in the code and 64 slots on the JVM. Hence 65. The system property kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer changes that default for every channel in the process. It is @DelicateCoroutinesApi, and its KDoc calls it a "last-ditch effort" for hot fixes. Write the size at the call site instead.

Check yourself before the Try it: what does the probe print for buffer(1)?

try.title: Count the emits that return
steps: Open AheadProbe.kt. Before you run it, write down a number for each of the seven lines, including handMadeBuffer(10), the KDoc's sketch.
Run it with the command below and compare.
Run it again with -Pargs=8 added. That sets kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer to 8 before any channel exists. Which line changes?
Run the Java twin, AheadProbeJava. It puts a SynchronousQueue or an ArrayBlockingQueue between two threads. Predict its four numbers first.

code.title: AheadProbe.kt
code.html: package workbench.flows.l04 import kotlinx.coroutines.CompletableDeferred import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.consumeEach import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.produce import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.buffer import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking // The ledger writer is stuck on posting 1 (a row lock). How far does the settlement reader get? private suspend fun probe(label: String, op: (Flow<Int>) -> Flow<Int>) = coroutineScope { var returned = 0 // emits that have returned in the reader val unlock = CompletableDeferred<Unit>() val posted = mutableListOf<Int>() val reader = flow { for (seq in 1..200) { emit(seq); returned = seq } } val writer = launch { op(reader).collect { posted += it; if (posted.size == 1) unlock.await() } } delay(100) // let the reader go as far as it can val ahead = returned unlock.complete(Unit); writer.join() println("%-22s emits returned while the writer held posting 1: %3d posted: %d".format(label, ahead, posted.size)) } // The buffer KDoc's own sketch of what buffer(n) does: a second coroutine and a channel. @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) private fun <T> Flow<T>.handMadeBuffer(n: Int): Flow<T> = flow { coroutineScope { val channel = produce(capacity = n) { collect { send(it) } } channel.consumeEach { emit(it) } } } fun main(args: Array<String>) { // -Pargs=8 sets the JVM-wide default size of a BUFFERED channel before anything reads it args.firstOrNull()?.let { System.setProperty("kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer", it) } runBlocking { probe("plain") { it } probe("buffer(0)") { it.buffer(0) } probe("buffer(1)") { it.buffer(1) } probe("buffer(10)") { it.buffer(10) } probe("handMadeBuffer(10)") { it.handMadeBuffer(10) } probe("buffer()") { it.buffer() } probe("buffer(UNLIMITED)") { it.buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED) } } }

alt.title: AheadProbeJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.flows.l04; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.SynchronousQueue; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; import java.util.function.Supplier; // Closest Java equivalent of Flow's buffer(n): a BlockingQueue between two threads. // Java blocks a thread where Kotlin suspends a coroutine; the counting is the same. public class AheadProbeJava { static void probe(String label, Supplier<BlockingQueue<Integer>> belt) throws InterruptedException { BlockingQueue<Integer> queue = belt.get(); AtomicInteger returned = new AtomicInteger(); // put() calls that have returned CountDownLatch unlock = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread reader = Thread.ofPlatform().daemon().start(() -> { try { for (int seq = 1; seq <= 200; seq++) { queue.put(seq); returned.set(seq); } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); Thread writer = Thread.ofPlatform().start(() -> { try { queue.take(); // posting 1 ... unlock.await(); // ... is stuck behind a row lock for (int i = 2; i <= 200; i++) queue.take(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); while (reader.getState() != Thread.State.WAITING) Thread.sleep(5); // reader blocked in put() Thread.sleep(50); int ahead = returned.get(); unlock.countDown(); writer.join(); System.out.printf("%-26s puts returned while the writer held posting 1: %3d%n", label, ahead); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { probe("SynchronousQueue", SynchronousQueue::new); // like buffer(0) probe("ArrayBlockingQueue(1)", () -> new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1)); // like buffer(1) probe("ArrayBlockingQueue(10)", () -> new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(10)); // like buffer(10) probe("ArrayBlockingQueue(64)", () -> new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64)); // like buffer() } }

try.expect: Plain 0, buffer(0) 1, buffer(1) 2, buffer(10) 11, handMadeBuffer(10) 11, buffer() 65, buffer(UNLIMITED) 200, and every posting arrives. With -Pargs=8, only buffer() changes, to 9. The Java twin prints 1, 2, 11 and 65: the same counting, with a blocked thread where Kotlin has a suspended coroutine.

sections.h: When the belt is full, the overflow policy decides who loses
sections.html:
Everything so far used the default policy, BufferOverflow.SUSPEND. When the belt is full, send waits, so the reader waits. Nothing is lost, and the reader is never more than n + 1 ahead. The other two policies never wait. When the belt is full they throw a value away.

Here are 200 FX ticks arriving while the repricer is stuck on tick 1:

Operator The repricer sees What the full belt did
buffer(10) all 200 made the feed wait
buffer(10, DROP_OLDEST) 1, then 191 to 200 pushed the oldest plate off the far end
buffer(10, DROP_LATEST) 1 to 11 dropped each new plate in the bin
conflate() 1 and 200 one plate stand: each new plate replaces the one on it

Tick 1 is in every row because the repricer had it in its hands before the flood started.

conflate() is buffer(CONFLATED), and the library turns CONFLATED into capacity 0 with DROP_OLDEST. A drop policy can't work with zero slots, so the channel gets exactly one. That rule sets a trap. A teammate wants "the newest 64 if the ledger falls behind" and writes buffer(onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST). The capacity defaults to BUFFERED, and the Channel KDoc says what that means with a drop policy: "If a different BufferOverflow is specified, Channel(BUFFERED) creates a channel with a buffer of size 1". So the line is conflate() under another name, and the probe receives [1, 200]. If you mean 64, write buffer(64, DROP_OLDEST).

Conflation only loses values that arrive while the collector is busy. A repricer that takes 50 ms, behind a feed that ticks every 100 ms, sees every tick.

So pick the policy by what a lost value costs. A stale FX rate is worth nothing once a newer one exists, so the repricer may conflate. A dropped ledger posting is money that reconciliation finds missing days later. Ledger postings get SUSPEND, always.

Reactor makes the same trades under other names, and you used them in lesson 7 of the reactive track:

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: Reactor's onBackpressure operators
rates.onBackpressureLatest();
rates.onBackpressureBuffer(10, r -> {}, BufferOverflowStrategy.DROP_OLDEST);
postings.onBackpressureBuffer(10);                    // full: the stream fails
Kotlin
rates.conflate()
rates.buffer(10, BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST)
postings.buffer(10)                                   // full: the reader suspends

In the probe the first two match their Flow twins exactly: [1, 200] and [1, 191..200]. The third doesn't. Reactor's bounded buffer with no strategy cancels the source and fails with OverflowException: The receiver is overrun by more signals than expected (bounded queue...). Flow's bounded buffer has no failure mode. It makes the producer wait.

Check yourself: what does buffer(0, DROP_LATEST) deliver in the same probe?

code.title: DropPolicies.kt
code.html: package workbench.flows.l04 import kotlinx.coroutines.CompletableDeferred import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.buffer import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.conflate import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking // 200 FX ticks arrive while the repricer is stuck on tick 1. Which ticks does it see afterwards? private suspend fun policy(label: String, op: (Flow<Int>) -> Flow<Int>) = coroutineScope { val unstuck = CompletableDeferred<Unit>() val seen = mutableListOf<Int>() val ticks = flow { for (tick in 1..200) emit(tick) } val repricer = launch { op(ticks).collect { seen += it; if (seen.size == 1) unstuck.await() } } delay(100) unstuck.complete(Unit); repricer.join() val shown = if (seen.size > 6) "${seen.take(3)} ... ${seen.takeLast(2)}" else "$seen" println("%-40s saw %3d ticks: %s".format(label, seen.size, shown)) } fun main() = runBlocking { policy("buffer(10) SUSPEND") { it.buffer(10) } policy("buffer(10, DROP_OLDEST)") { it.buffer(10, DROP_OLDEST) } policy("buffer(10, DROP_LATEST)") { it.buffer(10, DROP_LATEST) } policy("conflate()") { it.conflate() } policy("buffer(onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST)") { it.buffer(onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST) } policy("buffer(0, DROP_LATEST)") { it.buffer(0, DROP_LATEST) } }

The subscriber requests one tick, // holds it while 200 arrive, then requests the rest. Everything runs on the main thread. public class DropPoliciesJava { static void policy(String label, UnaryOperator<Flux<Integer>> op) { List<Integer> seen = new ArrayList<>(); Throwable[] error = new Throwable[1]; BaseSubscriber<Integer> repricer = new BaseSubscriber<>() { @Override protected void hookOnSubscribe(Subscription s) { request(1); } // stuck on tick 1 @Override protected void hookOnNext(Integer tick) { seen.add(tick); } @Override protected void hookOnError(Throwable t) { error[0] = t; } }; op.apply(Flux.range(1, 200)).subscribe(repricer); repricer.request(Long.MAX_VALUE); // unstuck String shown = seen.size() > 6 ? seen.subList(0, 3) + " ... " + seen.subList(seen.size() - 2, seen.size()) : seen.toString(); System.out.printf("%-48s saw %3d ticks: %s%s%n", label, seen.size(), shown, error[0] == null ? "" : "\n" + " ".repeat(49) + "ERROR " + error[0].getMessage()); } public static void main(String[] args) { policy("onBackpressureBuffer(10, t -> {}, DROP_OLDEST)", f -> f.onBackpressureBuffer(10, t -> {}, BufferOverflowStrategy.DROP_OLDEST)); policy("onBackpressureBuffer(10, t -> {}, DROP_LATEST)", f -> f.onBackpressureBuffer(10, t -> {}, BufferOverflowStrategy.DROP_LATEST)); policy("onBackpressureLatest()", Flux::onBackpressureLatest); policy("onBackpressureDrop()", Flux::onBackpressureDrop); policy("onBackpressureBuffer(10)", f -> f.onBackpressureBuffer(10)); } }

try.expect: Flow: buffer(10) all 200, DROP_OLDEST [1, 191..200], DROP_LATEST [1..11], conflate() [1, 200], buffer(onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST) also [1, 200] (one slot), and buffer(0, DROP_LATEST) [1, 2]. Reactor matches the first three, onBackpressureDrop() gives just [1], and onBackpressureBuffer(10) delivers 11 and then fails with "The receiver is overrun by more signals than expected (bounded queue...)".

sections.h: Buffers next to each other fuse into one channel
sections.html:
buffer(10).buffer(20) doesn't build two belts. It builds one belt with 30 slots, and the probe counts 31 emits. Every operator that is built on a channel (buffer, conflate, flowOn, channelFlow, produceIn) first looks at the flow it was called on. If that is also a channel flow, it adds no coroutine. It merges its settings into the one that is already there. The library calls this fusion. Picture short belt segments snapped together into one belt with one sticker on it.

The merge rules are short:

  • Two explicit sizes add up: 10 + 20 is 30.
  • buffer() without a size gives way to an explicit one, so buffer(10).buffer() has 10 slots and buffer().buffer() still has 64.
  • A policy other than SUSPEND replaces everything before it. buffer(10).conflate() is plain conflate(), and the 10 is thrown away. conflate().buffer(10) is a 10-slot belt that drops the oldest.
  • flowOn shares the channel too. buffer(5).flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) and flowOn(Dispatchers.IO).buffer(5) are both one channel, filled on IO, with 5 slots.

You can watch it happen, because these channel flows print their settings in toString():

buffer(10).buffer(20)    ChannelFlowOperatorImpl[capacity=30]
buffer(10).conflate()    ChannelFlowOperatorImpl[capacity=0, onBufferOverflow=DROP_OLDEST]
conflate().buffer(10)    ChannelFlowOperatorImpl[capacity=10, onBufferOverflow=DROP_OLDEST]
buffer(5).flowOn(IO)     ChannelFlowOperatorImpl[context=Dispatchers.IO, capacity=5]

Treat that string as a peek under the hood. It is a debug aid, not an API, and any release may change it. When it matters, test the behaviour instead: count the emits that return while the collector is stuck, as the lab does.

One line in the docs reads the other way. The conflate KDoc says that if a buffer size was given before it, "the buffer size is unchanged". In 1.11.0, buffer(10).conflate() delivers [1, 200] in the probe, exactly like conflate(), and its toString() shows capacity 0. The buffer KDoc matches the code: a buffer call with a non-SUSPEND policy "overrides all immediately preceding buffering operators". I read the conflate sentence as ambiguous rather than wrong, and I don't rely on it. When I want ten slots that drop the oldest, I write it in one call: buffer(10, DROP_OLDEST).

Check yourself: what single channel does buffer(10).buffer(5, DROP_LATEST) become?

Your extra line shows capacity=5, onBufferOverflow=DROP_LATEST.

sections.h: With collectLatest, a new value cancels the old block and waits for it
sections.html:
The FX repricer moves to collectLatest, so a new rate cancels the repricing in progress. Each cancelled repricing must release a quote lock first, which takes 50 ms that can't be cancelled. Ticks arrive every 100 ms and a repricing takes 300 ms. When does the feed emit tick 3?

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: switchMap cancels the inner; a cancel is a signal, so the release can only be fired off
rates.switchMap(rate -> reprice(rate)
        .doOnCancel(() -> quoteLocks.releaseAsync(rate).subscribe()));
Kotlin
rates.collectLatest { rate ->
    try {
        reprice(rate)                                                // 300 ms
    } catch (e: CancellationException) {
        withContext(NonCancellable) { quoteLocks.release(rate) }    // 50 ms
        throw e
    }
}

Most people say 300. The virtual clock says 350, and the run ends at 700 instead of 600:

t=100 emit 1, start 1
t=200 emit 2, cancelled 1 (ChildCancelledException)
t=250 cleanup of 1 finished, start 2
t=350 emit 3, cancelled 2
t=400 cleanup of 2 finished, start 3
t=700 done 3

collectLatest is mapLatest(action).buffer(0).collect(), and mapLatest is a thin wrapper over transformLatest. Its core is a short loop. A producer coroutine collects the upstream, and for each new value it cancels the previous block, joins it, and only then launches the new one:

flow.collect { value ->
    previous?.apply { cancel(ChildCancelledException()); join() }    // wait until the old block has finished
    previous = launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) { collector.transform(value) }
}

The join() is the surprise. Tick 1's cleanup must finish before tick 2's repricing starts. And this loop body runs inside the upstream's collect, so the join() also sits inside the feed's emit. The feed can't start its next delay(100) until the old block has cleaned up. Picture a cashier tearing up a half-written receipt when a new order comes in. She finishes shredding before she starts the new receipt, and the cook waits at the hatch meanwhile. Reactor's switchMap gives emits at 100, 200 and 300 and ends at 600, because a Reactor cancel is a method call that returns at once and there is no suspending cleanup to wait for.

Two rules follow. Keep the cancelled path short. And use the Latest family only for work you can throw away. Repricing a checkout is pure: a cancelled repricing costs nothing. Posting an FX revaluation entry per rate is a side effect: a cancelled block may have written half of it, and a skipped rate is never posted. That pipeline gets buffer().

Cancelling yourself behind a belt has its own surprise. A collector that never suspends calls cancel() on its own job at value 3. Behind buffer() it still receives 66 values in all, and behind buffer(10) it receives 12. The values already on the belt keep coming, because receiving from a channel that has elements doesn't suspend, and emitAll checks for cancellation once, before its loop. A collector that does I/O or calls delay sees the cancellation at its next suspension, so this bites only CPU-only collectors. Add .cancellable() after the buffer. It checks before every emit, and the count drops to 3.

try.title: Time the shredding
steps: Open LatestJoin.kt. It runs on virtual time. Predict the time of emit 3 and of done 3 before you run it.
Run it. Then change the cleanup's delay(50) to delay(150) and predict again.
Read the second half of the output: a collector that never suspends cancels itself at 3. Predict each count first.
Run LatestJoinJava, the switchMap twin, in real time.

code.title: LatestJoin.kt
code.html: package workbench.flows.l04 import kotlinx.coroutines.CancellationException import kotlinx.coroutines.NonCancellable import kotlinx.coroutines.cancel import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.Flow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.buffer import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.cancellable import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.collectLatest import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.flow import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.test.runTest import kotlinx.coroutines.withContext // A repricing that is cancelled must release a quote lock first: 50 ms that can't be cancelled. private fun repricingTimeline() = runTest { val t = { testScheduler.currentTime } flow { for (tick in 1..3) { delay(100); println("t=${t()} emit $tick"); emit(tick) } } .collectLatest { tick -> println("t=${t()} start $tick") try { delay(300); println("t=${t()} done $tick") } catch (e: CancellationException) { println("t=${t()} cancelled $tick (${e::class.simpleName})") withContext(NonCancellable) { delay(50) } // release the lock println("t=${t()} cleanup of $tick finished") throw e } } } // A collector that never suspends cancels itself at 3. What else reaches it? private suspend fun cpuOnly(label: String, f: Flow<Int>) = coroutineScope { val seen = mutableListOf<Int>() launch { f.collect { seen += it; if (it == 3) cancel() } }.join() println("%-30s the collector got %d values after cancelling at 3".format(label, seen.size - 3)) } fun main() { println("== collectLatest: cancel the old block, wait for it, then start the new one") repricingTimeline() println("== cancel() behind a buffer, with a collector that never suspends") runTest { val src = flow { for (i in 1..100) emit(i) } cpuOnly("flow { }", src) cpuOnly("flow { }.buffer(10)", src.buffer(10)) cpuOnly("flow { }.buffer()", src.buffer()) cpuOnly("flow { }.buffer().cancellable()", src.buffer().cancellable()) } }

alt.title: LatestJoinJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.flows.l04; import reactor.core.publisher.Flux; import reactor.core.publisher.Mono; import java.time.Duration; // Closest Java equivalent of collectLatest: Reactor's switchMap. A new tick cancels the // repricing in flight. Real time, so expect a few ms of drift. public class LatestJoinJava { static long t0; static boolean quiet; static void log(String msg) { long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; String line = String.format("t=%3d (about %3d) %s", ms, Math.round(ms / 50.0) * 50, msg); if (!quiet) System.out.println(line); } static void run() { t0 = System.nanoTime(); Flux.range(1, 3) .delayElements(Duration.ofMillis(100)) .doOnNext(tick -> log("emit " + tick)) .switchMap(tick -> Mono.delay(Duration.ofMillis(300)) .doOnSubscribe(s -> log("start " + tick)) .doOnCancel(() -> log("cancelled " + tick)) // a signal: nothing waits for cleanup .thenReturn(tick)) .doOnNext(tick -> log("done " + tick)) .blockLast(); } public static void main(String[] args) { quiet = true; run(); // a silent first run loads the classes, so the timings below are clean quiet = false; run(); } }

try.expect: emit 3 at 350 and done 3 at 700. With a 150 ms cleanup, tick 2 starts at 350, the feed emits tick 3 at 450, and tick 3 is done at 900 ms. The CPU-only collector gets 0 extra values from flow { }, 9 behind buffer(10), 63 behind buffer(), and 0 once .cancellable() follows the buffer. The Reactor twin emits at about 100, 200 and 300 ms and finishes at about 600 ms: its cancel doesn't wait for anything.

analogy: A kitchen and a dining room with a conveyor belt between them. Without a belt, the cook carries each plate to the table and stands there until the diner has eaten. buffer(n) hires a second cook and installs a belt with n slots: the cook keeps plating until the belt is full, so n plates wait and one is in the diner's hands. The overflow policy is what happens at a full belt: the cook waits (SUSPEND), the oldest plate is pushed off the far end (DROP_OLDEST), or the new plate goes in the bin (DROP_LATEST). conflate() swaps the belt for a single plate stand. The analogy breaks at fusion. Two real belts in a row hold the plates of both, and nothing on the second belt can erase the first. Two buffers in a row snap into one belt whose length is the sum, and a drop policy at the end replaces the belts before it.
world: Your FX service reads ticks from a Kafka topic and reprices open checkouts. conflate() or mapLatest is right there: a quote at a rate that has already moved is worth nothing, and repricing has no side effects. The nightly settlement import reads the acquirer's file and posts to the Oracle ledger. When a long transaction holds a row lock for two seconds, buffer(64) lets the reader stay 65 postings ahead and then makes it wait, so memory stays flat and nothing is lost. Put a drop policy there and a lock wait becomes missing money that reconciliation finds days later. Check the Kafka side too: a consumer that bridges records into a flow through a callbackFlow already has a 64-slot channel inside, and the same fusion rules decide what a buffer after it does.
mistake: Writing buffer(onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST) and believing it keeps the newest 64 values. The default capacity is BUFFERED, and a BUFFERED channel with any drop policy has exactly one slot, so the line behaves like conflate(). People make this mistake because buffer() alone is 64, and adding a policy looks like it changes only what happens when those 64 are full. A close cousin is buffer(10).conflate(), which is also plain conflate(), because a drop policy overrides the buffers before it. The fix is to say both things in one call: buffer(64, BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST). And before you pick any drop policy, ask what one lost value costs. For ledger postings the answer is always too much, so they get the default SUSPEND.

compare.title: The same loss policies in Kotlin Flow and in Reactor

java.title: Reactor
java.html: Flux<Posting> everyPosting = postings.limitRate(64); // demand in batches of 64; nothing is dropped Flux<Rate> newestOnly = rates.onBackpressureLatest(); // one slot, the newest replaces it Flux<Rate> lastTen = rates.onBackpressureBuffer(10, r -> {}, BufferOverflowStrategy.DROP_OLDEST); Flux<Rate> firstTen = rates.onBackpressureBuffer(10, r -> {}, BufferOverflowStrategy.DROP_LATEST); Flux<Rate> failFast = rates.onBackpressureBuffer(10); // full: OverflowException Flux<Quote> quotes = rates.switchMap(fx::reprice); // a new rate cancels the old call

kotlin.title: Kotlin Flow
kotlin.html: val everyPosting = postings.buffer(64) // full: the reader suspends val newestOnly = rates.conflate() // one slot, the newest replaces it val lastTen = rates.buffer(10, BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST) val firstTen = rates.buffer(10, BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST) // no failFast: a bounded Flow buffer never errors, it makes the producer wait @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) val quotes = rates.mapLatest { fx.reprice(it) } // cancels, joins, then starts the next

compare.note: The drop policies match one for one, and the probe gives the same lists in both. The machinery underneath differs. Reactor's backpressure is a number sent upstream with request(n), so limitRate reshapes demand and onBackpressureBuffer(n) has to decide what to do when a source ignores it: by default it fails. A cold Kotlin flow can't overflow, because emit doesn't return until the collector is ready. Loss is possible only where something puts a channel between two coroutines, and that is exactly what buffer, conflate and flowOn do. Two more differences show up in this lesson. Adjacent Flow buffers fuse into one channel with combined settings. And mapLatest joins the cancelled block before it starts the next one, while switchMap just sends the cancel.

worked.title: Pick the buffering for three pipelines in one service

steps.say: The checkout service reprices open baskets from an FX feed. Ticks come every 100 ms, a repricing takes 300 ms, and only the newest rate matters. A repricing that has started may finish. That is conflation.
steps.code: val quotes: Flow<Quote> = rates .conflate() // 1. one slot: a busy repricer skips to the newest rate .map { fx.reprice(it) } // 2. runs below the slot, in the collector's coroutine

alt.html: // Closest Java equivalent: keep the newest rate, reprice one at a time Flux<Quote> quotes = rates .onBackpressureLatest() // 1. one slot: a busy repricer skips to the newest rate .concatMap(fx::reprice, 1); // 2. one repricing at a time, asking for one rate at a time

steps.say: The basket page shows the price while the customer types an amount. A stale repricing should stop at once, and repricing has no side effects. Cancel it. In virtual time this finishes only the newest of three ticks, at 600 ms.
steps.code: @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) // mapLatest is experimental in 1.11.0 val shown: Flow<Quote> = amounts .mapLatest { amount -> fx.reprice(amount) } // a new amount cancels, joins, then starts again

alt.html: // Closest Java equivalent: switchMap cancels the inner call when a new amount arrives Flux<Quote> shown = amounts .switchMap(fx::reprice);

steps.say: The settlement import posts every record to the ledger. Nothing may be lost, and memory must stay bounded when a row lock stalls the writer. The default policy does both. The reader can get 65 postings ahead, then it waits.
steps.code: settlementFile.postings() .buffer(64) // SUSPEND: a full belt makes the reader wait .collect { ledger.post(it) } // nothing dropped, at most 64 waiting

alt.html: // Closest Java equivalent: a bounded queue between the reader thread and the writer BlockingQueue<Posting> belt = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(64); Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> settlementFile.postings().forEach(p -> putQuietly(belt, p))); // blocks when full while (true) ledger.post(belt.take());

steps.say: Review the teammate's version of the import, which was meant to "keep the newest 64". It keeps one. Under a two-second lock it posts posting 1 and the last one read, and silently drops the rest. Replace it with step 3.
steps.code: settlementFile.postings() .buffer(onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST) // BUFFERED + a drop policy = ONE slot .collect { ledger.post(it) }

alt.html: // Closest Java equivalent of the bug: Reactor's latest-only buffer settlementFile.postingsFlux() .onBackpressureLatest() // one slot, the newest replaces it .concatMap(ledger::post, 1) .blockLast();

lab.title: Build a belt by hand, then buffer FX ticks and ledger postings
steps: Run the tests once. All 11 fail. Read the test names in BufferingTest: they are the spec, and every timing is in virtual milliseconds.

In Belt.kt, write belt(capacity) without calling buffer(): flow { coroutineScope { ... } } with a Channel<T>(capacity), a launch that collects the upstream into it with send and closes it in a finally, and a for loop over the channel that calls emit.
In Buffering.kt, write everyRate, latestRate and cancelStale. Each is one operator and at most one map. Predict each test's virtual time before you run it.
Fix towardsLedger. The tests say the reader may run exactly 64 postings ahead and must never lose one.
Run the tests until all 11 pass, then run them once more.
hints: If belt(10) reports 0 emits, the upstream still runs in the collector's coroutine. The collect { slots.send(it) } must be inside the launch.
If a belt test hangs and then times out, the for loop is waiting for more values. Close the channel when the upstream's collect returns, in a finally.
mapLatest needs @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) in 1.11.0. Without it the compiler warns but still builds.
For towardsLedger, the default policy is the right one. You only need the right number of slots.
lab.done: All 11 tests in BufferingTest pass, twice in a row.

drill.title: Write buffer(n) from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page and the lab. Write fun <T> Flow<T>.myBuffer(n: Int): Flow<T> with flow { }, coroutineScope, a Channel and launch. Then answer without running anything: behind myBuffer(3), how many emits return while the collector is stuck on its first value? And behind myBuffer(3).myBuffer(3), built from your function rather than the library's?

answer.html: fun <T> Flow<T>.myBuffer(n: Int): Flow<T> = flow { coroutineScope { val slots = Channel<T>(n) launch { // 1. a second coroutine runs the upstream try { collect { slots.send(it) } } // send waits only when all n slots are full finally { slots.close() } // 2. lets the loop below end } for (value in slots) emit(value) // 3. our coroutine hands each value on } } // myBuffer(3): 3 on the belt + 1 in hand = 4 emits return. // myBuffer(3).myBuffer(3): your function doesn't fuse, so it is two belts and three coroutines. // The middle coroutine holds one value too: 3 + 1 + 3 + 1 = 8. The library's buffer(3).buffer(3) // fuses into one channel of 6 slots, so 7.

alt.html: // Closest Java equivalent: a producer thread and a queue with n slots (n >= 1 here) static <T> void myBuffer(Iterable<T> upstream, int n, Consumer<T> downstream) throws InterruptedException { BlockingQueue<Optional<T>> slots = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(n); Thread producer = Thread.ofVirtual().start(() -> { // 1. a second thread runs the upstream try { for (T v : upstream) slots.put(Optional.of(v)); // put blocks only when all n slots are full slots.put(Optional.empty()); // 2. the end marker lets the loop below end } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } }); for (Optional<T> v = slots.take(); v.isPresent(); v = slots.take()) downstream.accept(v.get()); // 3. producer.join(); }

recap: buffer(n) runs the upstream in a second coroutine that sends into a channel with n slots. With the default SUSPEND, the producer gets n + 1 emits ahead: n on the belt and one in the collector's hands.
buffer(0) still adds a coroutine, so it is 1 ahead. buffer() is Channel.BUFFERED, 64 slots on the JVM, so 65 ahead.
DROP_OLDEST, DROP_LATEST and conflate() never wait; they drop. buffer(onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST) has one slot. Ledger postings get SUSPEND only.

Adjacent channel operators fuse into one channel: explicit sizes add, and a drop policy replaces what came before. buffer(10).conflate() is conflate(). toString() shows the result, but test the behaviour.
collectLatest and mapLatest cancel the old block and join it, so a slow cleanup delays the next block and the producer. Use them only for work you can throw away.
A collector that never suspends and cancels itself behind a buffer keeps receiving what is on the belt. .cancellable() after the buffer stops it.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why the settlement import uses buffer(64) while the FX repricer uses conflate(), and why buffer(onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST) isn't a good middle ground for both. Explain it with the belt picture and the numbers from this lesson.
explain.answer: A buffer runs the upstream in a second coroutine and puts a belt between it and the collector. With buffer(64) and the default SUSPEND policy, the reader can get 65 postings ahead of a stuck ledger writer, 64 on the belt and one in the writer's hands, and then its send waits. Memory stays bounded and no posting is lost, which is what the ledger needs, because a dropped posting is missing money. The FX repricer is different: a quote at an old rate is worthless once a new rate exists, so conflate() is fine. It is a single plate stand where a new rate replaces the one waiting, and a repricing that has started still finishes. buffer(onBufferOverflow = DROP_OLDEST) looks like "keep the newest 64", but with the default BUFFERED capacity a drop policy gives a one-slot channel. Under a stall it posts posting 1 and the last one read, which is conflate() with a misleading name. It's wrong for the ledger, and for FX it just says conflate() in a confusing way.

deeper.html:
The class behind buffer, conflate and flowOn is ChannelFlowOperatorImpl, an internal subclass of ChannelFlow. Its fuse method does the merging. The new context is context + this.context, so for each context key the setting nearest the source wins, which is why two adjacent flowOn calls keep the first one. If the new policy is not SUSPEND, it overwrites the capacity and policy (the source comment says "this additional buffer never suspends => overwrite preceding buffering configuration"). Otherwise the capacities combine: BUFFERED gives way to an explicit size, two explicit sizes add up, and a sum that overflows Int becomes UNLIMITED.

buffer checks its arguments with require. buffer(-5) fails with "Buffer size should be non-negative, BUFFERED, or CONFLATED, but was -5", and buffer(Channel.CONFLATED, BufferOverflow.DROP_LATEST) fails with "CONFLATED capacity cannot be used with non-default onBufferOverflow".

Other operators are channel flows too, and they fuse with a buffer placed right after them. channelFlow { } prints as ChannelFlowBuilder[capacity=-2], and channelFlow { }.buffer(3) resizes the builder's own channel. mapLatest { } prints as ChannelFlowTransformLatest[capacity=-2], which is why its KDoc says it is "buffered by default". flatMapMerge { } prints as ChannelFlowMerge[concurrency=16, capacity=-2]; the next lesson takes it apart.

StateFlow already behaves as if conflate() were applied, and the KDoc says applying conflate to it has no effect. Lesson 7 of this track looks at why.

Reactor's limitRate(10) looks like buffer(10) in the probe: the source got 10 ahead, where Flow's count is 11 because the Flow probe counts emits that returned. The mechanism is different: limitRate batches the demand it sends upstream. It asks for 10, then for 8 more each time 75 % of a batch has been used.
